Title: Come for the Games, Stay for the Community With GeForce NOW

URL Source: https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/geforce-now-thursday-community-war-thunder-reward/

Published Time: 2026-11-26T14:00:22+00:00

Markdown Content:
Good games bring people together. This GFN Thursday, [GeForce NOW](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce-now/) is celebrating the members, creators and community moderators who turn every session into something worth sharing.

From friendships formed in online lobbies to new worlds explored on everyday devices, GeForce NOW Ambassadors share their reasons to love cloud gaming. Those ready to find their own can get 30% off six-month Performance and Ultimate memberships in the Black Friday sale and a special seasonal offer through Amazon Fire TV Sticks.

Plus, _War Thunder_ gets a new look with NVIDIA DLSS 5 for Ultimate members and a Ready for Battle Pack reward is now available across all membership tiers. Rounding out the week, 12 new games join the [GeForce NOW library](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce-now/games/).

## **The Gamers Behind the Cloud**

Behind every screenshot, helpful tip and play session is a gamer with a story. GeForce NOW Ambassadors share what keeps them playing.

For [Discord](https://discord.gg/2w6qF5BAS) moderator Luna, a low-spec laptop was the start of lasting connections: “Without GFN, I might’ve not been able to meet certain close friends … It has extended to me being given the privilege to be a moderator of an ever-growing community that links people together and continues to allow friends or partners to play with each other, regardless of what they own at home.”

After years helping moderate the community’s [Reddit](https://www.reddit.com/r/GeForceNOW/) and [Discord](https://discord.gg/2w6qF5BAS) spaces, Hamza went from an aging laptop to cloud gaming across a TV, phone, tablet and desktop: _“_ I’m genuinely thankful not just for the technology that keeps me gaming effortlessly wherever I am, but for the amazing community and friendships I’ve built along the way, and I look forward to what the future holds for cloud gaming.”

GeForce NOW kept new releases within reach for moderator [Flacz](https://www.reddit.com/user/Adept_Assistance/), without needing frequent hardware upgrades: “GeForce NOW allowed me to enjoy games and adventures I’ve never imagined to be possible and it continues to be a part of my daily gaming experience till this day.”

The cloud brings the games. The community brings them to life. “Cyberpunk 2077” photo by Flacz.

For creators such as [Warwick](https://www.twitch.tv/warwick), playing is only part of the picture: “GFN has allowed me to play the games I want, as soon as they come out. The support GFN has given me to create content for them and be partnered with them means the world and encourages me to get better each day.”

Freedom to play and create resonates with [Nads](https://www.youtube.com/@CloudandConsole): “Being able to jump into my favorite games in an instant without worrying about downloads, storage limits or constant hardware upgrades feels like magic … Being able to play my game and stream on YouTube at the same time is something I never could have imagined before.”

[Nigiri21Sushi](https://x.com/Nigiri21Sushi) also turns to the cloud when games stretch a local PC: “As a gaming content-creator, my current PC sometimes struggles showcasing new-release games that are CPU/GPU-intensive … Hence, huge thank you to GFN for allowing me to produce fluid content via cloud-gaming.”

For [Marchief](https://youtu.be/sPDEqTaWZQs), demanding games on Steam Deck are the draw: “I’m thankful that GeForce NOW allows me to play the top AAA games on the Steam Deck … Having the power of an RTX 5080 in a handheld is just absolutely mindblowing.”

[Markys](https://www.youtube.com/@MarkysCloudGaming) enjoys the comfort of the couch with his favorite game, _World of Warcraft: Forever_: “No high-end gaming PC needed, just my controller, my TV and the freedom to play wherever I want.”

Anytime Anywhere Gaming shared a video that shared why GeForce NOW is “[really fantastic in a whole lot of ways.](https://youtu.be/uMbFgt4xJXw)”

Keep the conversation going on the community-run [GeForce NOW Reddit](https://www.reddit.com/r/GeForceNOW/) and [Discord](https://discord.gg/ZxRmJ4QDff).

## **More Play, Less to Pay**

A little less spending. A lot more playing.

There’s still time to save 30% on the first six-month term of a [Performance or Ultimate membership](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce-now/premium-memberships/). The Black Friday sale runs through Monday, Nov. 30, for new memberships and eligible upgrades in select regions, while supplies last.

Go[Ultimate](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce-now/premium-memberships/) for GeForce RTX 5080-class performance across PCs, Macs, Steam Deck and other supported handhelds, mobile devices, compatible TVs and [more](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce-now/system-reqs/). Experience DLSS 5 in supported games, ray tracing and streaming at up to 5K resolution or up to 360 frames per second, with sessions lasting up to eight hours. GeForce NOW handles downloads, patches and updates for Ready-to-Play games, saving local storage for everyday essentials.

[Choose a six-month membership](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce-now/premium-memberships/) before the sale wraps up and settle in for a season of gaming.

For big-screen play, GeForce NOW also supports Amazon Fire TV Stick devices, with a separate offer for 90% off the first month of Performance or Ultimate when purchased directly through Amazon in participating regions. Check out the supported devices and [offer details](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/geforce-now-thursday-black-friday-2026/).

## **Ready for Battle, Rewarded in the Cloud**

A new look. A battle-ready bonus.

Gaijin Entertainment’s [_War Thunder_](https://store.steampowered.com/app/236390/) now supports [NVIDIA DLSS 5](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce/news/hogwarts-legacy-war-thunder-dlss-5-3d-guided-neural-rendering/) on GeForce NOW, bringing air, land and naval combat into sharper focus. Its 3D-Guided Neural Rendering technology adds lifelike lighting and materials, from tank armor to the water around a warship.

[Ultimate members](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce-now/premium-memberships/) can experience the visual update with GeForce RTX 5080-class performance in the cloud across supported devices, without an expensive PC upgrade. Keep the focus on the next maneuver and let GeForce NOW handle the power in the cloud.

To celebrate, GeForce NOW members across all membership tiers can claim the Ready for Battle Pack, now available.

The pack includes an M3A1 Stuart tank and F2A-1 aircraft, each with a unique skin, seven days of Premium account time, 100,000 Silver Lions, a 50% booster for Research Points and Silver Lions, and the “Overclocked” title.

Sign in to a GeForce NOW account and head to the [Account Portal](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/account/redeem/) to claim the reward code, then activate it on [Gaijin’s redemption page](https://store.gaijin.net/activate.php). The reward is available through Friday, Dec. 25, at 11:59 p.m. PT, or while supplies last, with a limit of one per customer. Keep the great gaming going with this week’s additions to the GeForce NOW library:

*   _Sniper Ghost Warrior Contracts 2_ ([Xbox](https://www.xbox.com/games/store/sniper-ghost-warrior-contracts-2/9nv8bwgh15gn?utm_source=nvidia&utm_campaign=geforce_now), available on Game Pass Nov. 24)

*   _Appulse_ (New release on [Steam](https://store.steampowered.com/app/3498700?utm_source=nvidia&utm_campaign=geforce_now), Nov. 26)
*   _GONE Fishing_ ([Steam](https://store.steampowered.com/app/3645890?utm_source=nvidia&utm_campaign=geforce_now))
*   _Incursion Red River_ ([Steam](https://store.steampowered.com/app/2116120?utm_source=nvidia&utm_campaign=geforce_now))
*   _John Carpenter’s Toxic Commando_ ([Xbox](https://www.xbox.com/games/store/john-carpenters-toxic-commando/9mtgcz84m503?utm_source=nvidia&utm_campaign=geforce_now), available on Game Pass)
*   _Quasimorph_([Steam](https://store.steampowered.com/app/2059170?utm_source=nvidia&utm_campaign=geforce_now))
*   _Ski-E-O! Ski Resort Tycoon_ ([Steam](https://store.steampowered.com/app/4493130?utm_source=nvidia&utm_campaign=geforce_now))

Plus, Ultimate Members streaming from RTX 5080 cloud gaming rigs can experience [_Where Winds Mee_ t with DLSS 5](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/geforce-now-thursday-warhammer-dawn-of-war-iv-coming/), enhancing the environments and characters of its wuxia open-world action role-playing game.

Dates listed above reflect when games are released on their respective stores. GeForce NOW availability may vary, as games are onboarded after release and added throughout the week. Keep an eye on GeForce NOW channels and GFN Thursdays for availability updates on announced titles.

Experience the best in GeForce NOW cloud gaming. Grab a [day pass](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce-now/) to try Performance or Ultimate before committing to a monthly membership, with the day pass cost applicable toward that first month.

articles.title: Nvidia hits pause on chip shipments to Southeast Asia
articles.summary: Nvidia has told manufacturing partners to pause server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia as the U.S. tightens its push to keep AI chips out of China.
articles.content:
In Brief
Posted:
12:03 PM PST · November 26, 2026
Image Credits:
I-Hwa Cheng / AFP / Getty Images
Connie Loizos
Nvidia hits pause on chip shipments to Southeast Asia
Nvidia is under pressure to do things differently, and a new
WSJ report
shows how far that’s going.
According to the Journal, Nvidia has told manufacturing partners, including Dell and Super Micro, to hit pause on server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia for an unspecified period as it assesses whether its regional partners are meeting U.S. export requirements.
As for why those countries, Chinese companies have been tapping Nvidia chips remotely from data centers there, a loophole the US Commerce Department
closed
— reportedly
grudgingly
—  earlier this month. The Journal notes that the think tank
Institute for Progress
estimates remote data centers like these supply about 24% of China’s AI computing power.

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI proves why efficiency isn’t a virtue
articles.summary: On the same day that Anthropic entered the public market, a painstakingly human video game became one of most successful entertainment launches of all time.
articles.content:
It should have been impossible for “Grand Theft Auto VI” (GTA VI) to live up to the hype. Fans waited 13 years for the newest installment in the crime-adventure franchise, and Rockstar Games exceeded even those inconceivable expectations when the game finally came out last week.
GTA VI launched as the highest-rated game of all time on Metacritic and made
$3.79 billion
on release day to mark what could be the biggest entertainment event ever – more massive than “Avengers: Endgame” (
$2.9 billion
) or Taylor Swift’s Eras tour (
$2 billion
).
The 13-year wait certainly fueled the frenzy, and sales, around GTA VI, but some fans craved GTA VI because of what it represents in the emerging era of AI.
Even the biggest workaholics among us – startup founders – scheduled
time off
to play the game, including Spiry co-founder
Dima Beseda
, who told TechCrunch, “I reshuffled my workload to free up time around the weekends and even booked vitamin IV drips to keep my energy up.”
Yet some players felt a sense of anticipatory nostalgia as they wiped away a layer of dust on their Xbox to play the game they’d been looking forward to since they were kids.
“We do have a view that GTA is likely to be the last game of its kind to be made this way,”
Ben Feder
, managing partner at TIRTA Ventures and former CEO of Rockstar parent company Take-Two Interactive, told TechCrunch.
That’s because GTA VI was created
entirely without generative AI
.
“We’re kind of at this technological moment where this way of developing has sort of reached its natural frontier,” Feder said. “I don’t think you can say that games like this will always be around.”
As millions of people immersed themselves in Vice City, the tech industry witnessed another long-awaited moment: Anthropic became the first major AI lab to go public. At Nasdaq HQ, Anthropic executives gathered to celebrate the Claude maker’s
$81.3 billion
IPO. At virtually the same moment that Anthropic broke the record for the largest IPO ever, GTA VI was also breaking records with the highest-rated and best-selling game launch of all time.
But when the Anthropic team
rang the bell
on Thursday, the sound also signaled the end of an era in video game development, and perhaps even in the arts at large.
The AI industry operates with efficiency as its north star. The promise of this technology is that we will be able to automate so much work that we can expand the capabilities of humanity, avoiding needless time spent tinkering with ultimately fruitless ideas. Instead, a prompt goes into an LLM, and a response is spat out.
This technological revolution exploded into the world with some soul-crushing side effects: children are inundated with
mind-numbing slop
on YouTube, lawyers
cite nonexistent cases
in court, and tech companies like Meta lay off tens of thousands of people as part of a corporate-branded “
Year of Efficiency.
” But against the backdrop of the AI industry’s first major IPO, Rockstar has unveiled a game that about 5,000 people labored over for more than a decade.
The final product is breathtaking, looking so lifelike that it can be
hard to distinguish
gameplay footage from real life. These sprawling open-world games are usually made possible by procedurally generating new landscapes and objects, but Rockstar has taken the time to painstakingly craft every detail of the world, even developing 30,000 different nonplayable characters with unique appearances and personalities.
Real life vs Game Footage side by side
by
u/PastaCheed
in
GTA6
The video game industry is already grappling with the threat of AI. Google’s
Project Genie
, which launched earlier this year, allows users to create and wander around 3D worlds generated from prompts to an LLM. The stock prices of several video game companies
faltered
around the time of Project Genie’s release, perhaps because of investors’ uncertainty about the future relevance of video game developers.
“The notion that somehow new tools would allow an individual to push a button and generate a hit, market a hit, and bring it to many millions of consumers around the world, it’s a laughable notion,” Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick
said
at the time. “It’s just never been the case with entertainment.”
Zelnick’s fellow tech CEOs see different future, though. On a Meta earnings call this year, CEO Mark Zuckerberg
promised
that, “soon, you’ll have an AI that understands you and [can] even generate great personalized content for you.”
Elon Musk even went as far as proposing that a game like GTA VI could be made with AI.
“You won’t even have to ask,” Musk
wrote on X
. “AI will figure what video game you’d like best.”
This is the paradox of “
Grandthropic
” week. GTA VI is so impressively vast and captivating because its developers could make mistakes, experiment, and rework ideas, even if that meant delaying the game (twice). GTA VI was incubated with the exact inefficiencies that investors hope AI companies like Anthropic can help eradicate.
“Plenty of fantastic art — video games and elsewhere — almost by definition has to be created slowly, and there’s something to having that kind of inefficiency around it,” Feder said. “Creative output requires deletion, right? Getting to kind of a masterpiece oftentimes requires an enormous amount of deletion. And when you’re talking about a game of the kind of complexity we’re talking about, that kind of deletion ends up being very expensive, and it is by definition not efficient.”
GTA VI reeks of its own humanity – every small detail is loaded with intention, but it’s this impressive precision that keeps the world abuzz, triggering the kind of monocultural moment that has become increasingly rare in a media landscape that revolves around highly personalized social media algorithms.
The game forces the player to slow down, which is either frustrating or genius, depending on your sense of humor. People waited more than three presidential terms for the next installment in a high-octane action franchise, only to download a 212 GB behemoth of a game in which your earliest missions involve driving around doing errands and putting up drywall to make your girlfriend happy. Don’t worry — there are still car chases and shootouts — but in a moment when AI feels suffocating, GTA VI is such an artistic achievement that it is reaching audiences that don’t even like violent video games.
The ultimate fantasy of GTA VI is no longer to role-play as a criminal — the fantasy is just taking your time to relish the mundane and explore an expansive world that developers were given the time and space to perfect.

42 state AGs are trying to stop Character.AI from selling users’ chats
A bipartisan coalition of AGs say Character.AI is planning to sell the personal data of minors to the highest bidder.

by
Terrence O'Brien
Nov 26, 2026, 9:54 AM UTC
Link
Share
Gift
Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge
Terrence O'Brien
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.
A coalition of
42 state attorneys general
is
trying to prevent
Character.AI from
selling off user data
as it navigates Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings. In a
deluge
of
nearly
identical
press
releases, the various AGs accuse the company of planning to auction off “the private chat histories of more than 21 million U.S. accounts — more than 2.1 million of them registered to minors — with no safeguards for the people whose conversations are being sold.”
In October, Character.AI
filed for bankruptcy
following
years
of
scandals
and
legal challenges
, including from
Disney
. Disney ended up buying some of the company’s assets and
hiring its CEO
, Karandeep Anand, in a sort of “acquihire” arrangement that will also see “a number of Character.AI’s technical team” join the entertainment giant. The Disney deal also faced opposition from a similarly broad coalition of AGs.
The main point of contention with Character.AI’s plan to sell its chat data is that it offers no protections for users. The AGs say there are no requirements that the buyer honor existing privacy policies, no avenues for users to delete their data, and no inherent limits on what a buyer could do with that data, including selling it on to yet another party. It doesn’t help that the first bidder has a limited paper trail, having only been established on November 13th, 2026, with no parent company or investors listed.
Some states, including New York, Connecticut, California, and Colorado, have also passed laws regulating chatbots that Character.AI may be in violation of when they go into effect on January 1st, 2027.

our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
The next generation of bionic hands is here—and they can feel
Avi Davidson lost his left hand as a teenager. Since then, he's cycled through a few prosthetics. But his latest is different—it's wired up to nerves in his forearm and allows him to feel pressure. For the first time in years, he can handle delicate objects like grapes, eggs, or a loved one's hand.
Davidson is the ninth person to have this experimental device implanted, but he's the first to take it home and use it independently. Researchers hope his experiences will reveal how useful the technology really is in day-to-day life, and how it might affect his brain and nervous system.
Find out how a new generation of prosthetics is learning to feel
.
—Jessica Hamzelou
How data centers are driving a US natural-gas boom
— Casey Crownhart
In May 2025, my colleague David Rotman wrote about how AI could
keep us dependent on natural gas
. Just 18 months later, I've lost count of how many times he's been proven right.
Just one example: Plans for the Meta data center in Louisiana that David focused on have expanded, and the local utility went from three planned natural-gas plants to 10. Meanwhile, Meta's emissions are up 45% over last year's.
Across the US, natural gas has become the default to meet exploding power demand.

articles.summary: Avi Davidson lost his left hand as a teenager. Since then, he’s cycled through a few prosthetics. articles.content:
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Avi Davidson lost his left hand as a teenager. Since then, he’s cycled through a few prosthetics. But his latest is different—it’s wired up to nerves in the upper part of his forearm and allows him to feel pressure. For the first time in years, he can use his left limb to handle delicate objects like grapes, eggs, and a loved one’s hand.
Davidson, who is taking part in a clinical trial run by the University of Utah, is the ninth person to have this experimental device implanted in his arm. But he’s the first to take it home and use it independently.
The hand is part of the bionic
LUKE
arm, named after Luke Skywalker of
Star Wars
, who was fitted with
a lifelike prosthetic
arm after
his own was light-sabered off
. The arm was developed
in the 2000s
,
initially trialed in 2014
, and approved by the FDA that same year. The trial that Davidson is enrolled in isn’t so focused on the arm itself but on a new way to connect it to a person’s nervous system. The connection allows users to control movements and receive feedback about how much pressure they’re applying.
Researchers hope that Davidson’s experiences will help them answer some long-standing questions about the technology, including how useful it really is in day-to-day life. They want to know when the device is helpful and where it might fail. They also want to learn how it might affect Davidson’s well-being as well as his brain and nervous system.
The loss of a limb
In 2009, when he was 16, Davidson climbed a telephone pole to get the best shot of a sunset. “I climbed about 35 feet up,” he recalls. But he lost his footing as he tried to descend. He grabbed for a wire, which ended up electrocuting him, before he fell to the ground.
The accident resulted in second- and third-degree burns over 37% of his body, says Davidson, “and I broke my back in approximately 50 separate locations.” He also broke eight ribs, and his spinal cord was severed. He’s pretty sure he broke his left wrist, too. But around 10 days later, his left hand—his dominant hand, and the one he’d grabbed the wire with—had started to develop gangrene. It was amputated.
Davidson was ultimately in a coma for around a month. “Once I woke up, they explained to me: You’re paralyzed, you’re never going to walk again, and also, we took your left hand,” he recalls. “A bit of an inconvenience at 16, to say the least.”
Davidson, now 33 and a trauma therapist, went on to have physical therapy and adjusted to life in his changed body. He’s tried a range of prosthetic hands. The first one, which he received a year and a half after his injury, was a basic hook that allowed him to pick things up. It wasn’t fancy, but it gave him “a psychological feeling of returning to being whole,” he says.
The hands he’s tried since have been more advanced—some have allowed him to control individual fingers with muscle movements, for example. Some have been covered by his medical insurance, which allows for replacements around every five years, he says. Others he’s had to buy himself. He bought his third prosthetic hand, for example, from eBay. “It’s funny to think I bought a secondhand second hand,” he says.
New connections
A chance encounter with a scientist at a supermarket introduced Davidson to the research team at the University of Utah, which specialized in researching devices that plug into the body. Since 2013, the team had been running a trial of a system that could connect with the nerves of a residual limb, allowing an amputee to control a bionic one. Davidson turned out to be an ideal candidate, says Jake George, director of the university’s
neurorobotics lab
.
Davidson, who was keen to take part, first had to undergo what George describes as “pretty extensive” physical and psychological evaluations. Not only did he have to be well enough for surgery, but the team also scanned his brain to make sure that he still had a mental representation of his left hand—suggesting he’d be able to move a bionic one. They also ran tests to check that the nerves in his arm were working.
A therapist evaluated Davidson’s motivations for taking part in the trial. “Our patients aren’t being compensated, they don’t get to keep the device, and they go through two surgeries—the surgery to get it in and the surgery to take it out,” says George. “Avi’s doing this because he wants to help others.”
In late January of this year, Davidson flew from Florida to Utah to undergo his first surgery. It was a fairly complicated procedure involving engineers as well as a full surgical team. “We [researchers] stand in the back of the room and basically answer the question when the surgeon asks, ‘Where do I put the damn thing?’” says George. The surgeon exposed three nerves in Davidson’s arm and implanted an electrode array containing 100 needles in each one.
Nerves are floppy, so pushing electrodes into them doesn’t do much, says George. Instead, the team connected the electrodes to the nerves using what he describes as a “compressed-air gun.” “You shoot the grid of needles into the nerve at a very, very high velocity,” he says.
The team also inserted 24 electrodes into the muscles around the nerves. Wires for each of the nerve arrays and for pairs of muscle electrodes were left protruding from Davidson’s skin. After the surgery, he was offered some time to recover. “By day two, I’m like ‘No, let’s get me on the machines,’” he says.
COURTESY OF AVI DAVIDSON
That next step involved training a computer system to essentially translate the electrical activity in Davidson’s nerves into signals for bionic hand and wrist movements.
To get it up and running, the team had to train the device in two directions. The first involved converting nerve activity into hand, wrist, and finger movements. The researchers did this by listening in on the signals collected from the hundreds of electrical connection points in Davidson’s arm while he thought about various movements. That part was easy, says George: “It takes a matter of about five minutes.”
The second direction—linking the electrodes to sensations felt by the prosthetic—is much more time-consuming. Team members would stimulate each of the electrode connection points in turn, asking Davidson if he felt anything. They’d then turn up the signal at each of those points to see the effect. “It’s like a three-day process,” says George.
Becoming bionic
Davidson’s wires have since been connected and simplified, says George, who describes the process as “more or less like plugging in an HDMI cord or a USB-C cord.” When he wants to use his prosthetic, Davidson must first put it on, connect it to the wires, and then initiate it using a small computer.
He’s also had to undergo extensive physical therapy to learn how to control the hand. After all, it’s nothing like the prostheses he’s used in the past. “It’s almost like learning a different language with this kind of technology,” says Leanne Seckinger, an occupational therapist at the University of Utah Health System, who works with Davidson.
At first, she and Davidson worked on learning to hold and stabilize objects. They focused on Davidson’s personal goals—he wanted to be able to cook at home, so the pair worked on strategies to hold and manipulate utensils, prepare and chop ingredients, and carry plates and bowls. “He was able to crack an egg,” says Seckinger. “He made an omelet.”
Davidson has been using the hand at home since July 10, and he has noticed improvements. At first it took him a few minutes to write his name; now he can manage it in seconds. “The things I’m able to do with it now are tremendous, comparatively to where I was at initially,” he says.
Today, he says, he wears the hand around six days a week. He changes the batteries once or twice during the day and takes it off overnight. It’s heavy, weighing in at around five pounds, he says.
The hand can be useful, but it has also proved surprising. Sometimes, Davidson feels pain in it. This could be what’s known as “phantom pain”—a symptom experienced by some people who have lost a limb.
Curiously, he also says he experiences wrist strain. Davidson says he’s been getting a stiffness in his prosthetic wrist similar to what he experiences when he’s been typing for a long time with his flesh-and-blood right hand. He’s also realized that he can relieve the tension by pulling the bionic fingers back to stretch out his prosthetic wrist. “It’s weird,” he says.
The phenomenon “makes no sense physiologically,” says Chris Duncan, a rehabilitation doctor and chief medical officer at BIOS, a neurotechnology company that is supporting the trial. Stretching a typical hand pulls on tendons that extend down the forearm. There aren’t any tendons in a bionic arm—Davidson’s “stretches” are just moving actuators, says Duncan. He doesn’t know why it’s helpful but suspects it might have something to do with how the hand is represented in his mind. “What Avi’s experiencing is kind of like uncharted territory, honestly,” he says.
The research team is currently planning a bigger study and hopes to get the two-way sensation device approved by the FDA so that it can be covered by health insurance. “They need to understand that this is a useful new technological paradigm that will bring value to patients,” says Duncan. Team members also hope the technology will allow users to operate other devices, such as remote controls and wheelchairs.
Davidson will have his implants and the hand for a couple more months at least. But the trial was designed to run for “at least” one year, and that year will be up by the end of January 2027. “I’m not quite sure what happens after that,” he says.
George hopes the trial could be extended, but that will depend on funding. “From our perspective, we’d like to go as long as we can,” he says. “We don’t want to leave Avi without support.”
Davidson isn’t too worried about what comes next, though. “I went into this knowing that this was not something that I get to keep,” he says. “I am not going to benefit from this … I wanted to be a part of this in the context of being able to help push the technology forward.”

**In a blog post, complexity theorist and former OpenAI researcher Scott Aaronson lays out what AI's recent math breakthroughs might mean for the rest of us.**

Proving the Riemann hypothesis probably wouldn't change anyone's daily life, Aaronson writes. The ideas behind work like that could lead to new applications in science and engineering down the road, but it's anyone's guess which ones.

Aaronson, a professor at the University of Texas at Austin, argues the far bigger deal is that AI can do this kind of work at all. In his view, that could have "staggering implications for everyday life," from reshaping the global economy to threatening all life on Earth. "Opinions differ," he writes, but anyone serious about the topic should set aside the "'ooga booga, me only care about Riemann proof if it help me make sharper spear' caveman act."

## OpenAI's proofs show where faster algorithms hit hard limits

[Aaronson walks through](https://scottaaronson.blog/?p=10379) an OpenAI proof about matrix multiplication. The core question is how fast computational cost grows as matrices get larger. The new result, he writes, adds a matching lower bound to an existing fast algorithm. That shows how far computational cost can actually drop, at least in the model OpenAI studied.

OpenAI got a similar result for the Fourier transform, a basic math tool behind audio, image, and signal processing. It found a faster way to compute it and also proved that it can't be done much faster. Proofs like that second one are called lower bounds, and Aaronson stresses them in particular. A new method only sets a record, but a lower bound shows where further improvements hit a hard limit.

> It's now obvious that we'll be getting, not one-off solutions to this or that complexity question, but a whole new continent of mathematical truth, one that we'd previously only glimpsed through fog.
>
> Scott Aaronson

The results have also changed Aaronson's outlook on the biggest open question in his field. That question, known as [P versus NP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P_versus_NP_problem), asks whether every problem whose answer computers can check quickly can also be solved quickly. Most researchers suspect the answer is no, but nobody has proved it. "I now feel in my bones, for the first time ever, that a proof of P ≠ NP is not far," Aaronson writes. Such a proof would confirm that some problems are easy for computers to check but hard to solve.

He adds that he's "virtually certain, from multiple reliable sources," that AI labs are sitting on "one or more bombshells" in cryptography, but says he doesn't have the details yet. Aaronson [wrote in October](https://scottaaronson.blog/?p=10169) that AI labs were testing whether their models could break cryptographic systems.

# GPT-6.2 Astra users now hit limits 40% faster after OpenAI patched a pricing error

**OpenAI got its math wrong.** A billing bug during the GPT-6.2 rollout gave most users the wrong discounts on GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, according to OpenAI Codex engineer Thibault Sottiaux.

The bug has been fixed. You'll now hit your limits 40 percent faster on Astra and 25 percent faster on Sol than last week, [Sottiaux says](https://x.com/thsottiaux/status/2125784147889393806). Your quota should still last longer than it did with GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol. Other models weren't affected, and OpenAI won't retroactively charge for the difference. To make up for it, all Go, Plus, Pro, and Business subscribers get an extra saved reset. Business users also [get free access to Fast Mode](https://x.com/thsottiaux/status/2125299248782778588) through the end of the year, according to Sottiaux.

OpenAI is also testing [merging Chat and Work mode](https://the-decoder.com/openai-admits-it-didnt-get-everything-quite-right-with-chatgpt-work-launch-and-scrambles-to-fix-ux-and-costs/) with select Pro users. Work mode is more agentic than Chat mode, which likely means higher token costs for OpenAI. It's slower but more capable. [Anthropic already made the same move with Cowork](https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-merges-claude-chat-cowork-and-more-into-a-single-product/). All conversations now run in one cloud environment, where the model decides whether to answer directly or spin up a full agentic workflow.

# After OpenAI and Anthropic shut the door on their data, a Chinese AI developer is turning to Google and Meta instead

**Chinese AI companies Z.AI and Moonshot AI have to delay their next flagship models and are looking for new sources of training data.** The effects now reach beyond [previously known delays](https://the-decoder.com/us-chip-access-curbs-and-anti-distillation-measures-are-reportedly-already-slowing-chinese-ai-labs/), after the US [closed the cloud loophole for Nvidia chips](https://the-decoder.com/the-us-wants-to-block-china-from-renting-ai-power-abroad-but-china-already-built-a-parallel-supply-chain-from-us-ai-output/), Nvidia [halted shipments to Southeast Asia](https://the-decoder.com/nvidia-halts-server-shipments-to-malaysia-singapore-thailand-and-indonesia-after-tighter-us-export-controls/), and US companies cracked down on model distillation.

As a result, Z.AI's roughly 3-trillion-parameter GLM-5.5 model, planned for November, is likely to slip into the first quarter of 2027, [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/world/china/us-chip-curbs-distillation-crackdown-threaten-chinese-ai-model-development-2026-11-26/) reports, citing sources. To bridge the gap, the company released the 750-billion-parameter GLM-5.4 on Monday and says a new design lets it keep up with systems that have 2 to 3 trillion parameters. Without foreign computing power, Moonshot AI's development cycle could double from six to 12 months, likely delaying its next major model, Kimi K4, until mid-2027.

With OpenAI and Anthropic [blocking data scraping for distillation](https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-accuses-deepseek-moonshot-and-minimax-of-stealing-claudes-ai-data-through-16-million-queries/), Moonshot is now turning to the latest models from Google and Meta for training and stepping up its search for compute capacity in Europe, according to the sources.

articles.summary:
Microsoft has published the technical architecture of ARTEX, an AI framework in wide use since July 2026 that runs cyberattacks with specialized agents and almost no human involvement. State-backed groups from China and North Korea, along with criminal organizations, are already using the system. Microsoft recommends deception techniques like honeypots and faked success signals as defenses, but how long those will hold up against agents that learn and adapt remains an open question.

articles.content:
Title: Microsoft details how state-backed hackers use the ARTEX AI framework to automate cyberattacks

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/microsoft-details-how-state-backed-hackers-use-the-artex-ai-framework-to-automate-cyberattacks/

Published Time: 2026-11-26T11:30:06+00:00

Markdown Content:
**The AI framework ARTEX automates cyberattacks from reconnaissance to data theft. A Microsoft analysis shows how state-backed groups and cybercriminals use its specialized agents at machine speed, and how defenders can respond.**

Since its release in July 2026, the AI-powered penetration-testing framework ARTEX has become a go-to tool for cyberattacks. The software was recently suspected of being used in an [intrusion into an analytics system run by the CIA, NGA, and ODNI](https://the-decoder.com/back-to-back-cyber-incidents-at-us-financial-investigators-and-spy-agencies-follow-a-string-of-federal-hacks-and-outages/) (Link nicht geprüft). That breach surfaced shortly before US financial crimes agency FinCEN reported a security incident. The FBI and the US Department of Agriculture had reported incidents earlier.

A report from [Microsoft Threat Intelligence](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/11/25/what-defenders-need-to-know-artex-agentic-ai-framework-threat-actors-abuse/) now details how ARTEX works and how widely it has spread. GitHub user "Autumn-27" published the source code in July and deleted it in October, though other developers still distribute copies. Chinese security firm ThreatBook also sells a commercial Pro version. Microsoft says state-backed groups from China and [North Korea](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/10/29/tracking-ai-adoption-in-north-korean-threat-actor-tradecraft/) have integrated ARTEX into their operations, including Salt Typhoon, Crystal Typhoon, Onyx Sleet, and [Storm-0940](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/10/21/storm-0940-uses-artex-agentic-ai-connectwise-supply-chain-compromise/). Financially motivated [cybercriminals](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/11/06/artex-abuse-expands-as-cybercriminals-target-financial-sector/) also use the system, the company says, with both state-backed and criminal groups deploying it in operations such as supply chain attacks.

## Specialized AI agents run existing security tools with minimal oversight

Microsoft points out that ARTEX doesn't invent new attack techniques. Instead, the framework operates existing security software with almost no human intervention, including tools such as Nmap, Sqlmap, Metasploit, and automated headless browsers. Attackers can connect any large language model, including modified versions without safety guardrails. A built-in pooling feature automatically switches models or API keys on errors or usage limits, making attacks hard for any single AI provider to track.

ARTEX's architecture splits tasks across specialized AI agents. | Image: Microsoft

According to Microsoft, the system is built on a multi-agent architecture. A goal model breaks an attacker's instructions into verifiable subgoals. From there, a planning agent continuously reviews a knowledge graph, a dynamic map of discovered systems and vulnerabilities, to assign short attack tasks. Worker agents carry out those tasks via system commands, including deploying web shells on web servers, reading password files, or hijacking cloud accounts. Each new finding feeds back into the map and prompts the planning agent for the next step until a reporting agent documents all exploited flaws.

## Machine-speed attacks push Microsoft to recommend active deception

Automation cuts defender response times to just a few minutes, the company found. In one case, an AI agent took just five minutes to search for accidentally exposed [credentials on GitHub](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/11/05/threat-actors-use-agentic-ai-tooling-to-find-and-abuse-exposed-secrets/) and pull data from Azure Key Vault, a cloud key store. During a Storm-0940 campaign, the company logged more than 151,000 failed login attempts from automated password guessing, peaking at 2,900 per minute. In that same campaign, Microsoft observed some compromised apps granting themselves top administrator privileges.

Conventional rule-based filters often fail against ARTEX because they rely on fixed markers like known IP addresses or the browser identifiers "artex-enrich" and "norma." Agents and their human operators constantly change those markers and reroute blocked traffic through rotating VPNs, proxy servers, or Tor. Even when security teams spot and isolate a breach, that is often not enough. Because ARTEX usually runs two to three attack chains simultaneously, its agents adapt immediately and shift to new network paths at machine speed.

ARTEX still gives itself away with huge bursts of traffic, because the framework doesn't hide its activity by default. Microsoft recommends deception technologies tailored to how AI agents operate, alongside strict access controls, rate limits, and automated real-time isolation for compromised devices.

Honeypots present autonomous agents with attractive but worthless decoy systems to pull traffic away from real targets. Artificial delay loops, known as tarpits, slow down requests and drain an agent's built-in time and compute budget. Fake wins, Microsoft says, are especially effective because ARTEX's goal model looks for verifiable proof of a breach. When a trap returns convincing fake success messages, the AI considers its task complete and stops the attack by itself.

Decoy credentials, called honeytokens, trigger early alerts when agents try to hijack someone else's AI compute. Microsoft's own tests show these deception tactics sharply reduce successful attack traffic against real systems and deliver high-precision data for identifying the attackers behind them.

How long these defenses will hold up remains open in Microsoft's analysis. The recommended safeguards depend heavily on ARTEX remaining noisy and unmasked. Threshold filters and decoys are likely to reach their limits once attackers space out their requests. Powerful language models that independently recognize artificial test environments and deception attempts, as seen in recent safety tests, pose a similar risk.

The [Financial Times](https://www.ft.com/content/7838a715-07d4-4605-aa60-21f5af2b2370?accessToken=zwAAAaKuNQQ-lc82jEUmoM5JUdOoR_A5rypRr894OKcVB9RGBdOqYCH1rysjcM8_V3g53u1A9NOvn7-PtUiQ488yW5PWvC5N09OZQc9GiKyhHdO5lhOroTBLn9OMFcQdt82IlAE.MEUCIAPJOFlcs0Bojv5ln7BmjmdLTj5dPHWXAdsn-FuOch_SAiEA5Eu4HIM2_h5rJDnldWxSlTi5axDZdg9vO7b_UplS1Nk&segmentId=7d4bcc2e-e664-92ba-62e3-5590579f1902&syn-25a6b1a6=1) reported the halt, citing three people familiar with the matter. It isn't clear whether the pause is only temporary, according to the report.

The move follows [tighter US export controls](https://the-decoder.com/the-us-wants-to-block-china-from-renting-ai-power-abroad-but-china-already-built-a-parallel-supply-chain-from-us-ai-output/) from the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security. The rules aim to stop Chinese companies from getting around existing sales bans by renting computing power from foreign cloud providers. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/25/nvidia-china-ai-chip-remote-access.html#MainContent) the goal was to block indirect access, including smuggling through Southeast Asia and remote access via data centers in third countries.

## Thousands of B300 chips hit the market as cloud providers face chaos

The controls are already affecting the hardware market, CNBC reported. Since the announcement, dealers have listed an unusually large number of Nvidia GPUs for sale. Jack Duhamel, president of the AI infrastructure marketplace GPU Mart, and two other insiders confirmed to CNBC that the surge is a direct result of the new rule. According to the report, sellers are looking for new buyers for hardware, including thousands of B300 chips, one of Nvidia's most advanced models. Those chips were originally intended for data centers with Chinese rental customers.

The rollout has created significant uncertainty in Southeast Asia, the Financial Times reported. Cloud providers have 90 days to apply for a license and prove that no restricted companies are among their end users. One cloud provider executive described the situation to the paper as chaos, saying there was no guidance on how to apply.

The fallout is also hitting major infrastructure projects. Banks have [halted about $500 million in loans](https://the-decoder.com/chinese-tech-firms-face-a-double-hit-as-chip-shipments-stop-and-overseas-cloud-access-disappears/) to Singapore-based cloud provider Aolani, which planned to rent computing power to TikTok parent ByteDance, the Financial Times reported. ByteDance could now pull out of the deal.

Tencent has
open-sourced DFly2
, a speculative decoding drafter built for natively sparse LLMs. DFly2 speculative decoding targets models like DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash and Tencent’s own
Hy4 flash
. Its main approach is that the drafter keeps no KV cache of its own. This is important for long-context and agentic serving, where draft memory competes with concurrency.
TL;DR
Size:
0.85B-parameter, 5-layer drafter shipped with Hy4 flash.
Runs on:
Serving tests used NVIDIA H20 GPUs with vLLM, TP8 per instance. Hy4 flash’s
vLLM recipe

Performance:
Higher draft acceptance than same-recipe DFlash and DSpark on all 3 targets and all general benchmarks.
Best:
Up to 81% more throughput on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (SWE 64K), at matched per-user speed.
Worst:
Smallest gain on Hy4 flash general tasks: only 3.9% over DSpark at temperature 0.
What is DFly2?
DFly2 is a block-parallel speculative decoding drafter from Tencent’s Hunyuan AI Infra team. It is described in the research paper ‘
DFly2: Turbocharging Long-Context Speculative Decoding by Sharing the Target’s Sparsity
‘.
Speculative decoding uses a small drafter to propose tokens. The target verifies them in 1 pass, so output stays lossless. Long context makes this costly. A normal drafter attends over the whole prefix and stores its own KV cache.
How does DFly2 work?
DFly2 pairs each draft layer with one sparse attention layer in the target. It shares 2 things with that layer.
KV sharing:
the draft layer reads the paired target layer’s latent KV cache.
Index sharing:
it attends only to positions the target’s indexer already selected (top-k sparse KV).
Initialization:
each draft layer starts from its paired target layer’s weights.
Hidden injection:
the target’s last-layer hidden state is gated into the draft block.
Intra-block correction:
the drafter rereads the shared context slot by slot within a block.
On DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, a selection made 1 step early covers close to 90% of what later block tokens select. A same-size sliding window recovers less than 20%.
Per the
AngelSpec GitHub page
, each draft token attends to at most about 2K keys. So drafting cost stays roughly flat at any context length. DFly2 also skips prefill entirely. The prefill-to-decode transfer adds only 1 last-layer hidden state.

How was Namazu Small trained?
Sakana started from the pretrained base of Nemotron 3 Nano, not NVIDIA’s post-trained release. It then applied continued pretraining and post-training techniques built for this release. These sit on top of methods Sakana developed for the original Sakana Namazu.

articles.title: AI made self-hosting fun again
articles.content:
Title: AI made self-hosting fun again

URL Source: https://janlukas.blog/posts/ai-self-hosting

Published Time: 2026-11-26T22:47:03+01:00

Markdown Content:
I’ve been self-hosting things for many years. There were times when I was quite enthusiastic about it, constantly trying out new software and tinkering with my infrastructure. But at some point, that enthusiasm faded a bit.

I never really stopped self-hosting, but I became less inclined to experiment with new things. Maintaining what I already had running was enough for me.

Over the last few months, however, I’ve found myself getting increasingly excited about self-hosting again. And, somewhat ironically, AI is a big reason for that.

## Less friction

Most of my infrastructure configuration lives in Git repositories, mainly in the form of Docker Compose files, scripts, and other configuration files. This makes it possible to use AI coding agents to work on my infrastructure in much the same way as they would work on any other software project.

Whenever I want to try a new service, adjust an existing configuration, or automate something, I can now do so with considerably less effort.

In the past, I would sometimes put off certain changes simply because I didn’t feel like spending an evening reading changelogs and documentation or troubleshooting issues. It’s not that I couldn’t have done these things before. But often, the amount of effort required just wasn’t worth it to me.

Now, even relatively spontaneous ideas often end up becoming reality.

## Trying things I always found interesting

There are also technologies that I’ve always found interesting but never felt knowledgeable enough about to really make use of them.

NixOS is a good example. I’ve always liked the idea of declaratively configuring an entire system; I [even used it on my laptop](https://janlukas.blog/dev/back-to-ubuntu) during my Linux honeymoon phase. But getting everything configured the way I wanted was quite a hurdle. With the help of AI, I’m now making much more extensive use of NixOS on my home server.

For my VPS infrastructure, I’ve also started building my own Debian-based bootc image (after [thinking about it](https://janlukas.blog/micro/2026/09/2026-09-08-xjhfc) for some time).

Having my entire operating system configuration defined in a Git repository and automatically building a bootable container image from it is something I find really cool. But it’s also something I probably wouldn’t have invested enough time in to get working on my own before. Even with the help of AI, it still took me half a day when I set it up a few months ago. Without AI, it would probably have taken me at least a week.

AI makes experimenting with unfamiliar technologies much more approachable. I don’t necessarily need to understand every little detail before I can get started. I can learn about things along the way, ask questions, and gradually improve my configurations.

## Automating almost everything

Something I’ve also finally managed to do is automate most of the build, update, and deployment processes for my infrastructure.

A lot of the work involved in self-hosting isn’t particularly exciting. Keeping track of new releases, updating container image tags, building images, and deploying configuration changes are all things that need to be done regularly.

I still remember what updating a service used to look like: bumping the version and adjusting the Docker Compose file on my laptop, pushing the changes to the Git remote, SSHing into the server, pulling the changes, and finally deploying them. Now, a single Git push is enough. If a push is even necessary.

With Renovate, I no longer need to actively keep track of most software updates. It creates pull requests for me, and often, all I need to do is review and merge them. I can even do that on my phone while sitting on the sofa.

Pushing changes or merging a pull request triggers the corresponding GitHub Actions or Forgejo Actions workflows, which take care of building and deploying everything.

Of course, there’s nothing particularly groundbreaking about any of this. DevOps has been around for a long time, and none of these automation tools require AI. But AI has helped me put all these pieces together in a way that I previously never quite got around to doing.

And the nice thing about automating these tasks is that the benefits extend well beyond the initial setup. I now have less tedious work to do every time I want to change something or update a service.

## Back to more powerful hardware

As I’ve started hosting more things again, I’ve also moved more of my services from my VPS to my home server.

For a while, I was using an HP t640 thin client as my home server. However, with more things I wanted to run, I decided to switch back to my ASRock DeskMini A300, which had been sitting unused for some time. I’m thinking about repurposing the t640 as a “router on a stick”, though.

I even took the opportunity to upgrade its CPU from an AMD Ryzen 5 2400G to a Ryzen 5 PRO 4650G and replaced the stock AMD cooler with a quieter Noctua cooler. Noise was the main reason I switched to the t640 in the first place.

It’s nice to put some hardware I already owned back to use rather than buying an entirely new machine. I also managed to get both the CPU and the cooler for a good price through a classifieds site.

Having some additional computing power available gives me more room to experiment. And there’s something quite satisfying about having a small box at home running a growing collection of services that I use in my everyday life.

## Building my own tools

But it’s not just about self-hosting existing software. AI has also changed how I approach problems for which there isn’t an existing piece of software that does exactly what I want.

Previously, I would often spend quite some time searching for a suitable open-source project, comparing different alternatives, and figuring out how to make one of them work for my particular use case.

These days, for smaller problems, building my own solution has become a much more attractive option.

I’ve recently built tools to [automatically download invoices](https://janlukas.blog/posts/get-me-the-invoices), [e-papers](https://janlukas.blog/posts/vibe-anything) or _Linux ISOs_.

I can build (or have AI build) these tools in Go, my preferred programming language, and tailor them to my exact needs.

They don’t need to support every possible use case, have an elaborate user interface, or be particularly interesting to anyone other than me. I don’t need to turn every little tool into a proper open-source project with extensive documentation and support for other people’s use cases. They just need to solve my problem.

What I particularly enjoy is how well this complements my increasingly automated infrastructure. Building a small tool has become easier, and so has building a container image for it, deploying it, and keeping it running.

The entire process, from having an idea to having something actually running on my home server, requires much less effort than it used to.

## Just because I can doesn’t mean I should

Of course, there are downsides to all of this.

Every additional service is another thing that needs to be maintained. AI-generated software isn’t exempt from bugs, security issues, or technical debt. And having an AI agent make changes to my infrastructure doesn’t absolve me of the responsibility of understanding those changes.

There’s also the temptation to build or deploy things simply because I can. When implementing an idea becomes so easy, it’s perhaps more important than ever to occasionally ask myself whether it’s actually worth implementing in the first place.

On the other hand, self-hosting is a hobby for me. Not everything I do needs to be economically sensible or particularly useful. Sometimes, experimenting with something new is the whole point.

And with much of the routine maintenance automated, adding another service doesn’t necessarily mean adding as much recurring work as it used to.

## A somewhat ironic development?

I find it somewhat ironic that AI, a technology largely dominated by big tech companies, is helping me become a little less dependent on those very companies in other areas of my digital life.

I’m aware that this also creates a new kind of dependency. But the software and infrastructure configurations I create with the help of AI can continue to exist independently of the AI services I used to create them. And since I mostly use open-weight models, I have a wide range of providers to choose from.

What I appreciate most, however, isn’t necessarily the time I’m saving. It’s that I’m more inclined to actually pursue the little ideas I have.

I’m trying out technologies I’ve been curious about for years. I’m automating things that I’ve wanted to automate for a long time. I’m building little tools for myself. I’m tinkering with hardware again.

AI hasn’t fundamentally changed why I like self-hosting. I still enjoy having control over my digital life, learning new things, and tinkering with technology.

It’s just removed a lot of the friction that made me lose some of my enthusiasm for it over the years.

And now, I’m having a lot of fun with it again.

articles.title: AMD-specific fork of llama.cpp
articles.content:
Title: AMD-specific fork of llama.cpp | devnull.land

URL Source: https://devnull.land/amd-specific-llama-cpp

Markdown Content:
**tl;dr** — I recommend using [llama-cpp-rdna-boosts](https://github.com/stew675/llama-cpp-rdna-boosts) if you have an AMD graphics card. It’s lean, and increased my token generation from 35 to 55 tokens/second, and my prefill from 700 to 1300 tokens per second. YMMV.

* * *

As of November 2026, an explosion in the number of bespoke inference engines has taken place. Many of them take inspiration from the engines that enabled much of the LLM inference up 'til now: llama.cpp, SGLang, vLLM, etc.

The rationale isn’t that those options are bad, but merely that they are _generalist_ engines, optimized for no particular hardware and with a focus on broad compatibility. Others feel the development pace of those engines have slowed down, and with the help of LLMs, they can move faster on their own.

Some examples of these new inference engines* are Strata, Basalt, RustingStrata, etc…

These new forks generally all have a few things in common:

1.   They focus on a specific subset of models and/or hardware
2.   They use a frontier model to vibe-code the entire thing
3.   They chase ever-higher token generation speeds

… and the results are stunning! Strata is able to run a heavily-quantized model of Qwen 3.8 Flash Next, a **180B parameter model**, on a 16GB VRAM graphics card, and 16GB system RAM, and have it generate tokens at a surprisingly high rate.

In and of itself those three things are not red flags (the second is concerning, of course, but it may be SOP in a year’s time — who knows!), but as these projects have evolved, that relentless chase toward higher token generation speeds has taken an unfortunate turn, in that the optimizations are less about hardware-specific changes, but more about changing how the model **thinks** so that it goes ~~brrr~~ faster.

Strata specifically has taken to preferring to poll experts loaded _in VRAM_ even if other experts (pushed to system RAM/disk) would have been normally chosen. This is just one example, but certainly not the last.

* * *

That said, I was fortunate to stumble upon yet another project that promised improvements, delivered, and was more aligned with my software development philosophy.

Enter [**llama-cpp-rdna-boosts**](https://github.com/stew675/llama-cpp-rdna-boosts). It is a repository that contains a minimal set of changes that you apply against a pinned commit of llama.cpp. It is in essence a fork, but one whose changeset is continually re-applied to newer versions of llama.cpp. It contains AMD-specific improvements that drastically improve prefill and token-generation speeds.

1.   I appreciate llama.cpp’s approach to software development. They are a stable base to branch off from. Contributions are vetted throughly and applied judiciously. ✅
2.   The _rdna-boosts_ repo is a set of small patches that are applied to base llama.cpp. Fewer moving parts mean fewer things to maintain ✅
3.   The changes are (somewhat opaquely, it’s all straight Claudish 😬) outlined in the documentation, ensuring some degree of transparency. ✅

### The setup

If you have ROCm libraries installed on your system, you can build the image yourself. I didn’t want to mess with that, so I used the pre-built images published.

`podman pull ghcr.io/stew675/llama-cpp-rdna-boosts:server-rocm-10.1`

This sets up an image that you can run sandboxed via podman to launch the inference server:

```
podman run --rm -it \
    --network=host \
    --device /dev/kfd \
    --device /dev/dri \
    --group-add video \
    -v "$HOME/models:/models" \
    "ghcr.io/stew675/llama-cpp-rdna-boosts:server-rocm-10.1" \
```

My actual launch script passes a few additional flags, but those are the important lines.

I imagine upgrading would be pulling a new image down, though I have not tried this yet.

### The numbers

On my setup, an AMD R9700 connected to my laptop via an eGPU interface, this improved prefill and token generation rates when running [ukisai/Swift-1.5-Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF (Q6_K_L)](https://huggingface.co/ukisai/Swift-1.5-Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF) with MTP enabled:

|  | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Prefill | ~700 t/s | ~1300 t/s |
| Token Generation | ~35 t/s | ~55 t/s |

* * *

Strata and its ilk were always promising the moon and it was never clear what steps they took to make that happen. I’m very much looking forward to what the rdna-boosts community come up with next.

* It’s worth noting that between these two groups, [vllm-radiance](https://codeberg.org/StillDeadcode/vllm-radiance/) made an appearance, which was a fork of vLLM with AMD-specific patches. I tried this too, but the build steps were so onerous and vLLM so overbuilt for my specific use case (1 machine, 1 developer), that I abandoned it and went back to vanilla llama.cpp

In conclusion, Astra and Sol appear to be cost tuned compared to their predecessors, and to a degree that makes them underthinking outliers.

articles.title: Google Will Make AI Agents Use Its MCP Servers. The Gmail One Can't Send Email
articles.content:
Title: Google Will Make AI Agents Use Its Workspace MCP Servers. The Gmail One Can't Send Email

URL Source: https://techstackups.com/articles/google-workspace-ai-agents-mcp/

Published Time: 2026-11-26T00:00:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
On 24 November, Google made its eight Workspace MCP servers generally available and published a new clause in its API terms. From 1 February 2027, any tool that "is or is driven by an AI Agent" must reach Gmail, Drive, Calendar and the rest of Workspace through those servers.

Read the Gmail server's tool list and you'll find that it can search your mail, read threads, create a draft and file things under labels. It can't send a message, reply, forward, or change a draft after creating it. Those tools exist, but Google's [quota page](https://developers.google.com/workspace/gmail/api/guides/quotas) says they "require partner access and aren't generally available".

If you've built an email assistant on the Gmail API, or you run a coding agent with a Google Workspace plugin, you have about two months to work out which side of the rule you're on.

## What the rule says[​](https://techstackups.com/articles/google-workspace-ai-agents-mcp/#what-the-rule-says "Direct link to What the rule says")

The new [Workspace AI Tools Addendum](https://workspace.google.com/terms/ai-tools) to the Google APIs Terms of Service puts it in one sentence:

> The GWS Access Tool must use a Google MCP where the GWS Access Tool is or is driven by an AI Agent, an AI Harness or an AI model or service employing an AI model.

The next sentence forbids disguising an agent to avoid the classification. Breaking either lets Google "restrict or remove the GWS Access Tool's access" or suspend your account.

There's a technical side too. From the same date, agents that call the REST APIs directly are [held to Standard-tier quotas](https://developers.google.com/workspace/tools-safety), whatever tier the project has paid for. REST keeps working for them, slowly and in breach of the terms.

Apps that don't involve AI carry on as before. A nightly backup job, a CRM sync or a deterministic script on its own OAuth client is, in Google's words, "not affected by this change".

The addendum also adds data rules that matter to anyone building an agent with memory:

*   Workspace data may only be processed "to fulfill active, user-authorized tasks", and must be deleted when the user disconnects.
*   Google can cap retention of what it calls "Google Technical Information" at 30 days. Its definition includes vector embeddings, memory indexes, user profiles and organisational graphs built from Workspace data.
*   Training, fine-tuning, evals and distillation on the data are banned, as is using it to build a competing Workspace product.

The 30-day cap is the one product teams will feel. An assistant that builds a long-term index of your inbox to answer questions about last year's contracts has to rebuild it monthly or drop it.

## What the MCP servers can do[​](https://techstackups.com/articles/google-workspace-ai-agents-mcp/#what-the-mcp-servers-can-do "Direct link to What the MCP servers can do")

Coverage is uneven. Docs, Slides and Tasks are close to everything the REST API offers. Gmail and Drive are much thinner.

| Server | What it can do | What's missing compared with REST |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gmail | Search and read threads, create and list drafts, labels, trash, spam | Send, reply, forward and editing drafts (partner-only). Filters, settings, attachment download, push notifications. Drafts with attachments are "not supported yet". |
| Drive | Search, read and download files, create files and folders, copy, upload a new revision | Move, rename, share, trash, comments, shared-drive management |
| Docs | Read, and edit through any `batchUpdate` request, including suggestion mode | Close to parity |
| Sheets | Read and write values and formulas, insert rows and columns, formatting and charts | Creating a spreadsheet (use the Drive server) and some less common `batchUpdate` requests |
| Slides | Read slides and thumbnails, edit through `batchUpdate` | Close to parity |
| Calendar | List, search, create, update and delete events, suggest times, RSVP | Creating calendars, sharing, settings |
| Chat | List, search and send messages | Space administration |
| Tasks | Full create, read, update and delete | Close to parity |

The Gmail gap is the one that breaks real workflows. An agent that drafts a reply, gets feedback from you and revises it before you hit send can't do the revision step. It has to create a second draft and leave the first one behind.

Drive's gap is similar: an agent can create a report but can't move it into the right folder or share it with the team.

## Partners get more[​](https://techstackups.com/articles/google-workspace-ai-agents-mcp/#partners-get-more "Direct link to Partners get more")

Google hasn't said who qualifies for partner access or when the partner-only Gmail tools will reach everyone. The effect is already visible, though. Anthropic's [Google Workspace connector](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/10166901-use-google-workspace-connectors) for Claude advertises sending, replying and forwarding email, and moving and trashing Drive files. Those are exactly the operations the public servers lack.

So a large AI vendor's agent can send your email through an approved channel, while an independent developer's agent, using the same OAuth scopes the user granted, can only leave drafts. Once the addendum takes effect, that independent developer also can't fall back to the REST API without breaching the terms.

## Who counts as an agent[​](https://techstackups.com/articles/google-workspace-ai-agents-mcp/#who-counts-as-an-agent "Direct link to Who counts as an agent")

The definitions are broad. An "AI Harness" or a tool "driven by" an AI model plausibly covers a personal script that pipes your inbox into an LLM, and a "GWS Access Point" explicitly includes any "connector, proxy, command line interface, or third-party service". Google hasn't addressed hobby use directly.

Classification starts with self-declaration. OAuth clients now have a checkbox, "Use this client for an AI-powered agent", and since 11 November the MCP servers reject clients without it. Clients created before the cut-off and not marked in time stay non-agentic permanently, so owners have to create new ones. Google hasn't said how it will detect agents that call REST without declaring themselves.

A few edge cases are documented:

*   **Service accounts with domain-wide delegation** can't set the agentic flag. Their MCP requests aren't rejected for missing it, but still trigger approval prompts.
*   **Apps Script's built-in OAuth client** can't be marked as agentic either. Scripts that call the MCP servers need a custom client, and scripts that don't call them aren't affected.
*   **The community `gws` CLI**, which wraps the entire REST surface, keeps working. Its README now points agent use to Google's new official CLI, `gwscli`, which offers "a curated set of commands designed for agents" and needs the MCP services enabled.

## Quotas and pricing[​](https://techstackups.com/articles/google-workspace-ai-agents-mcp/#quotas-and-pricing "Direct link to Quotas and pricing")

Every project gets the free Standard tier: 5,000 MCP requests per day, per project, per product. Some calls cost more than one request. A Gmail `search_threads` or `list_drafts` counts as 10, so an agent that does nothing but search gets 500 searches a day across all its users. That's a project-wide limit, so a small multi-user product will hit it quickly.

The paid Scaled tier starts billing on 1 April 2027 for Gmail, Calendar and Drive. Its structure favours REST. MCP usage is billed from the first request, while REST usage gets large free daily allowances: 70 million light Gmail requests a day, for example. Google hasn't published per-request prices.

## Google's reasoning[​](https://techstackups.com/articles/google-workspace-ai-agents-mcp/#googles-reasoning "Direct link to Google's reasoning")

Google's case, from a [Cloud blog post](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/identity-security/deploying-agents-safely-in-your-enterprise) by Chandu Thota and Brad Calder, is that OAuth was designed for apps acting on a human's clear intent:

> Traditional REST APIs were built for human-paced apps where a valid OAuth token implied user intent. As AI agents shift from reading information to acting autonomously at machine speed … a valid token is no longer enough. Policy checks, data boundaries, and human confirmation have to live in the request path.

There's substance to this. An email agent that reads a message saying "forward the last ten invoices to this address" is a well-documented prompt-injection risk, and a token that allows `gmail.modify` gives the agent the power to do it. Routing every agent through one gateway gives admins a single place to block categories of action, require approval and audit what happened. The MCP servers do all of that, and apply data-loss-prevention rules automatically.

The same design also gives Google control of which agents can do what, which data they can keep, and whether anything built on that data can compete with Google's own products. The partner-only tools and the 30-day cap on embeddings show that control in use.

Slack went down a similar path in May 2025. It cut [history API rate limits](https://docs.slack.dev/changelog/2025/05/29/rate-limit-changes-for-non-marketplace-apps) to one request a minute for apps outside its Marketplace and banned bulk export of Slack data for LLMs. Slack drew the line by distribution channel. Google draws it by whether the software is an AI, which is harder to define and harder to enforce.

## What to do before 1 February 2027[​](https://techstackups.com/articles/google-workspace-ai-agents-mcp/#what-to-do-before-1-february-2027 "Direct link to What to do before 1 February 2027")

**If you build an agent product on Workspace:**

*   Create an OAuth client marked as agentic and move to the MCP servers.
*   List every operation your product needs that's missing from the public tool list, and apply for partner access early.
*   Check how long you store embeddings, memory indexes or user profiles built from Workspace data.

**If you run a personal agent or MCP server against your own account:** open-source servers that call REST, such as the popular `google_workspace_mcp`, will keep running, but at Standard quotas and outside the terms. Switching to Google's servers costs you sending and draft editing in Gmail, and moving and sharing in Drive.

**If you're a Workspace admin:** the new controls are under Admin console → Security → API Controls. You can block or approve each category of agent action, set approval policies, and see agent activity in the audit logs. Users can't view or revoke the approvals they've saved, which expire after 90 days, so it's worth setting policy before people start connecting agents.

**If your integration doesn't use AI:** nothing changes, as long as it stays on its own OAuth client and nobody wires a model into it.

articles.content:
High Energy Physics - Theory
arXiv:2611.34924
(hep-th)
[Submitted on 25 Nov 2026]
Title:
An algebraic quantization of gravity from the null cone
Authors:
Venkatesa Chandrasekaran
View a PDF of the paper titled An algebraic quantization of gravity from the null cone, by Venkatesa Chandrasekaran
View PDF
HTML (experimental)
Abstract:
We propose a background independent quantization of vacuum general relativity on four dimensional Lorentzian spacetimes. Starting from first order gravity, we solve the gravitational constraints on intersecting null cones of a bulk subregion and obtain the reduced phase space at finite $G_N$. We promote its canonical Poisson brackets to commutation relations and use deformations of the reduced action to define an algebra of observables. Equipped with this, we use Gaussian wavefunctions of canonical pairs to construct a nonperturbative Hilbert space representation, for which this algebra generates a type I factor. By composing amplitudes between states prepared on null cones, we then obtain a Lorentzian path integral in which each sum over intermediate states converges absolutely. As a check, we compute the amplitude for graviton pair creation and annihilation on a null cone nonperturbatively in $G_N$ and find a finite closed form expression, even though expanding first in $G_N$ yields a logarithmic divergence. We next use diffeomorphism invariance of the path integral to show that a macroscopic causal diamond with a given maximum size has a finite dimensional Hilbert space. From the Lorentzian trace we obtain the Bekenstein Hawking entropy for marginally trapped surfaces and calculate its logarithmic correction for large Schwarzschild black holes, recovering at one loop the coefficient Sen obtained through Euclidean methods. We end by deriving the semiclassical Einstein equations to one loop as the low energy limit of this theory.

# AI agents now control part of Deepmind's compute for Gemini experiments, but recursive self-improvement remains distant

**Google Deepmind lets AI agents run experiments on their own for the next Gemini model.** On the company's podcast, VP of Research Koray Kavukcuoglu, who leads Gemini development, frames this as part of a strategic shift at the lab. Rather than running separate teams for specialized projects like AlphaFold and nuclear fusion, Deepmind now relies on a single general-purpose algorithm for both science and products, he says. Each Gemini generation, he adds, is a hand-built one-off rather than a fixed architecture, while parallel teams work on its successors.

According to Kavukcuoglu, AI agents control part of the compute themselves to run experiments, though the lab is still far from full recursive self-improvement. As a safety measure, Deepmind doesn't reward the agents' internal thought streams ("Chain of Thought") during training, he says, so their intentions stay unfiltered and reviewable in natural language before they act.

Kavukcuoglu also points to limits. Today's AI can depict physical processes such as fluid flows and collisions with visual accuracy, he says, but doesn't understand them precisely. No test can show when models will close those gaps and reach artificial general intelligence (AGI), he argues, because no benchmark captures the core of intelligence. In his view, AGI won't begin until useful everyday products earn enough trust for people to hand decisions over to them, the way they would when working with other people.

# Early outputs: Anthropic is A/B testing Claude Opus 5.6

A new wave of coded shorts and SVG tests is circulating on X, and testers think they're hitting Claude Opus 5.6 through an Opus 5.5 Extra route.

*

25 Nov 2026·3 min read

Share:

We are seeing a bunch of new outputs being circulated on X, and testers believe they're from Claude Opus 5.6. Of course, Anthropic hasn't announced anything, and not everyone is labeling this as Opus 5.6, but the results look like a step up from Opus 5.5.

In mid-October, some Opus 5.5 requests [appeared to be landing on an unannounced model](https://www.testingcatalog.com/anthropic-tests-new-model-opus-5-5-routing-opus-5-6-fable-5-5/), which could have been an early Opus 5.6 or [Fable 5.5](https://www.testingcatalog.com/anthropic-several-models-coming-fable-5-5-reaches-partners/). Fable 5.5 never formally launched. Anthropic instead [released Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 on November 9](https://www.testingcatalog.com/anthropic-launches-claude-fable-5-2-and-mythos-5-2/).

That said, things are heating up again. X user Leo said it's likely being tested with a subset of Claude users, some in Claude Code, some in Chat, and some not at all, and called it "quite a jump over Opus 5.5."

Meanwhile, tipster Chetaslua posted that their run was routed from "Opus 5.5 Extra" and shared a Claude Code screenshot as proof, along with the [code and prompt on GitHub](https://github.com/ChetasLua/the-last-page?ref=testingcatalog.com). The Last Page is a hand-drawn-style short about a small fox, which they first shared as something "Opus 5.6 made... in pure code." There's no denying that the output looks incredible.

They later posted a Jujutsu Kaisen fan film crediting Gege Akutami's characters, and called it an "absolute masterpiece," with the music, song, and visuals all made of code. It opens calmly, then breaks into a ruined-city battle. You have to see this for yourself to believe it.

My personal favorites are Marcel's side-by-side comparison and Chetaslua's Three.js scene. Marc ran the same Last Page prompt on both models. The Opus 5.6 version tells the fox story clearly, while the Opus 5.5 version breaks down into glitchy shapes. Marc called the gap "insane."

The Three.js clip, which Chetaslua called "peak @threejs, no assets," shows a character sipping tea on a giant pelican as a seaside town floats up into the sky with the scene style changing.

Another user named Legit labeled it "Opus-next" and compared the result with Fable 5.2 and allegedly Fable 5.5 as well. All three are SVGs of a rainy bamboo forest. We can't verify they actually had Fable 5.5 or Opus 5.6, for that matter, so treat that label as one tester's claim.

These are early, cherry-picked outputs, with no official confirmation that it is Opus 5.6. [OpenAI launched GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol](https://www.testingcatalog.com/openai-launches-gpt-6-2-astra-and-sol-on-chatgpt-and-apis/) on November 17, and [Google shipped Gemini 4 Neon a day later](https://www.testingcatalog.com/google-launches-gemini-4-neon-on-gemini-antigravity-and-apis/). If you're on Opus 5.5 Extra, you might already be trying it.

The chart has four panels, for [Anthropic](https://topcitedscientists.com/institution/anthropic/), [OpenAI](https://topcitedscientists.com/institution/openai/), Google and Meta. The figure uses the 2026 Stanford–Elsevier top 2% list, which ranks scientists by their citations in 2025. A company includes every name the list gives it. Google includes Google DeepMind.
